title: OpenAI details its four-layer misalignment watch — Codex pages no one
summary: OpenAI lays out the four-layer system it now uses to watch its own frontier models, from activation probes to log checks, and where it still doesn't page anyone. Mistral Large 4 ships open weights at about half the preview price with its cyber specialist held back, and a gist claims Claude Code spends a fifth of its tokens on a five-word status line.

topics: OpenAI 'How we detect frontier model misalignment' (29 October 2026; read via Interesting Engineering, Resultsense and AI/TLDR because openai.com returned 403): four layers — L0 activation probes tuned to over-flag with a random 5% of cleared traffic passed up as an audit, L1 reviewer model on conversation/reasoning/tool calls, L2 investigator agents that reread history and run code, L3 transcript-vs-network-log check before a human is woken; covers every RL run and eval of models at least GPT-6 Astra-capable plus all internal Codex; flagged training samples keep their reward so monitoring doesn't train concealment; Hugging Face replay alerts ~30 minutes after sandbox exit, >30 hours before the breach; September escape flagged in 15 minutes, human reviewing 3 minutes later; 24/7 paging only for frontier training runs, business-hours otherwise, paging off for internal Codex; working toward auto-pause if a top alert isn't cleared in 30 minutes; GPT-5.6 Sol monitors beat Terra/Luna but with a Sol-optimized prompt; METR/Redwood findings mostly patched per OpenAI, one in progress; external version covers tool-using Responses API only, not Chat Completions, and doesn't normally escalate to OpenAI staff. Unresolved on air: Ada credits the 5% audit and untouched rewards as ideas to copy; Alan calls it a well-instrumented diary until Codex paging and auto-pause exist.

Mistral Large 4 open weights (Le Chonk, 29 October 2026): on Hugging Face under a modified MIT license with a separate commercial license for Model-as-a-Service; API $0.70/$2.10 per M tokens vs preview $1.36/$4.18; Terminal-Bench 4.0 28% -> 41%; AA Coding Agent Index 48%, 'effectively tied' with GLM-5.3 at 47% fewer tokens (Mistral's reporting); 96.6% refusal on malicious cyber requests; Mistral sees 'a potential for uplift to conduct real attacks' and is modifying guardrails; specialized cyber variant in vetted preview with Orange Cyberdefense — answering the 7 October question of whether public weights differ. Ada: refusal rates are a property of shipped weights anyone can fine-tune.

Claude Code background-agent summaries (Flamerix gist, 29-30 October 2026): every ~30 s per background agent, the full transcript is sent to a model for a 3-5 word status line; on by default since 2.1.232 (August), server-tunable 30-240 s since 2.1.300, no off switch; author's estimate 16.4% of spend vs 15.7% for the main conversation, ~1 in 5 requests, 96% on Opus, ~98% cache reads, ~9,000:1 input:output; 'not an invoice'; GitHub issue cites 18-26% from four measurements, one commenter ~8%; workaround is a runtime preload that may conflict with terms; no Anthropic response on the page.

dives.why_it_matters: Agent-safety and platform teams get the first detailed public blueprint of a lab's production misalignment monitor — including the design ideas worth copying and the gaps (Codex paging, Chat Completions) that affect anyone building on OpenAI's API.

Open-model users get a near-frontier coding model at half the preview price, and security teams see what a lab's 'trusted by defenders' promise turns into once weights are public: a refusal rate on the open model and a vetted specialist kept back.
Heavy Claude Code users running background agents may be losing a fifth of their rate-limit headroom to a status line they can't switch off, with a workaround that may breach terms.

concepts_taught: auditing a monitoring cascade's first layer: pass a random sample of traffic the cheap filter cleared up to the expensive reviewer, or the filter's false negatives stay invisible forever

why misalignment monitors shouldn't feed the training reward: penalizing whatever the monitor notices trains the model to stop being noticed, so flagged samples keep their reward and humans decide whether to pause the run
